commenti.body: Stories endure longer than anything else. And through them, we touch on the thoughts of so many artists long gone without necessarily even knowing it. The closest thing to immortality.

I can think of no higher compliment for an artist than his or her art still being appreciated after the creator’s passing. After all, any work of art is meant to be filled with a message. That the message still lives on even after the body has passed is in a way a connection to those who we cannot communicate with any longer.

I went through a period of watching “actuality” film from the early years, and if anything that’s even more moving because they’re normal people doing ordinary things more than a century ago. The Lumiere Bros have a short film of the pigeons in the Piazza San Marco in 1896, and at some point a little kid walks by and you can’t not start thinking—did he live to see or even be in the Great War? Did he somehow see the 21st century? It could be those, it could be anything in between.

Anyway, less about artistry but they captured some very banal scenes that are now incredibly thought-provoking.

Good job. There shouldn’t be any ambivalence about loving the cinema, and diving into its rich history.

You should look into the new free streamers, movie-web, cataz, m4uhd, etc. there’s no reason to pay for all these DVDs : you’ll never be able to own all the movies you want to see.
I have access to a lot of streaming options but, when the movies I want to watch are not on one of them, I try to buy a DVD/Blu-Ray (if I can).

DM me if you want the links.

I applaud your love to the cinema. I am in the same boat: since 2021, I’ve seen 3,000 movies and the more I watch, the more I discover riches I missed.

>I was too young to fully appreciate them when they were alive and now, when I'm touched by their works, they're dead.

On the flip side, you're able to just focus on and enjoy their best work.  Had you experienced their works when they were originally released you may have had to live through years of their not-so-great stuff, or watch them slowly decline into awfulness.   

And who is to say you would have even been aware of them during their best period even if you were alive then?   It's not like everything was easily available in the past (although yes, mainstream films had huge audiences).  

Recently I discovered a song that I really really like by an artist who died long ago.  It was released when I was a child.  Even a decade or two after that there was pretty much zero chance I would have heard it in my life.   But jump forward years and I thankfully stumble on it.  

Enjoy your time machine that lets you travel throughout cinema's past.

Since the pandemic I have also watched old films with a melancholy feeling, feeling like I’m in the wrong era, like the best times to be alive have passed, and I’m here to tell you that you are possibly struggling with depression and possibly even OCD. For a couple of years, I didn’t want to engage with any media from today. It felt wrong. 

I’m not a doctor, nor an expert on the DSM, but if these feelings become overwhelming, you should try to book time with a therapist. It’s not dangerous by any means, and it’s not an emergency. It’s just something that can happen to people who are nostalgic, longing and wistful. I don’t want to put anything out there, this is all just highly relatable to me and when I spoke to someone about it, I gradually felt better over time. Death is a terrifying concept, and time moves way too fast. It’s a very common discomfort as you age.

If I may, your ambivalent feelings are pointless. If you like painting, music or litterature (judging by your study, I guess you are), there is no nostalgia or melancholy when you enjoy a Caravaggio, a Bacon or a Nicolas de Staël, there is no sadness to have deceased friend who still can show you, explain you things, tell you stories, make you feel deep emotions or understand though concepts. Kafka, Deleuze, Gary or Melville are friends of mine, they helped me to construct myself, they are always there for me, except when I need help for boxing my stuff during a removal. Same thing goes for cinema. Lang, Welles, Chabrol, Leone, Carmet, Delphine Seyrig, Silvana Mangano, Robert Mitchum, Anita Ekberg, Rochefort... they are immortals. Time and death  doesn't exist.

Althought, to me, what you're discribing apply when it comes to non-comedian watching the camera before they died. I don't know if you're familiar with Chris Marker, especially *Level 5*, but there is something heartbreaking when ghost are watching you, like the guy who jump from the top of the Eiffel Tower. Or Nicholas Ray in *Nick's Movie*, by Wenders... but this is a completly different story.

One more thing that is good with dead people, they cannot disappoint you, contrary to... Clint Eastwood, for example.

Contrary to the feeling of "living with ghosts", as if by watching these films you were performing a sort of necromancy, I would say that the temporal distance somehow adds a renewing beauty and enriches your experience, because it allows you to develop new perspectives on an artistic work. Not only can you realize things that went unnoticed at the time they were made, but also experience feelings/thoughts that have been partially lost. And even if they are dead, much like a finished book has nothing more to tell by itself, they become ever-changing through your enjoyment.

I want to watch movies like the old ones, the important ones and the ones that I can think about and talk about but I am just waiting for someone to come to my life. So that i can watch and still talk about it. I regret watching good movies in the past.

I wouldn’t claim to have watched more movies than the next person, but I do find myself reaching out towards hoping that a find an old good movie vs feeling excited about a new good movie.
Being also in the same age range, I suspect it could have something to do with nostalgia or age related something-something, especially if you work in a creative field or are someone that needs a ‘why’ for the things.
Just a speculation.

Interesting observations. What’s great about cinema is that the best of it is timeless, and great art might go out of fashion for a period, but then it can come roaring back into relevance and mean more in whatever present period we are in than it might have when it was originally made. It’s why we call some artists ‘ahead of their time’. 

The sadness I feel now watching old films comes I think from an understanding of where the industry is now, how tastes and the whole medium has shifted (tik tok kills me) and it doesn’t feel now as much of a continuum as just a compromise and lesser, fragmented form than what it used to be. This could also change again. But as we enter an era of less resources, more austerity, less risk taking, less audience participation, more passive viewing, more streaming, studios disintegrated … I don’t think the lines around the block to see a stellar smaller film , or even most big films , or the budgets to make them will be there - except as an exception rather than the rule. 

All the more reason to invest in being a fan these days.

I kinda get what you mean. When I was younger I generally had some interest in indie movies that progressed into French New Wave and generally older classic.   
Now I have this weird feeling that when I have time i'd rather invest in an older movie depicting times i've never experienced speaking in a way i've never experienced than look for some newer movies. I always find a way to back out from researching newer movies, not sure why. So yeah, not exactly the same, but still a weird experience with older movies.

> Had you experienced their works when they were originally released you may have had to live through years of their not-so-great stuff, or watch them slowly decline into awfulness. 

And not just *on*-set decline, you'd have to inevitably deal with *off*-set controversies and scandals in many cases. 

One of the nice things about old films is that the controversies and scandals of participants in many cases are finished and laid bare. So now you get to look at a director or actor and see who they became after the years of scandal and intrigue instead of potentially feeling like you have to weigh in on currently evolving situations. Maybe they became better people, or maybe they got even worse. Maybe they made amends, maybe they didn't. Maybe you can separate the art from the artist, maybe who they ended up being was so awful you can't do that.
